questions.q: What's the difference between json.dump() and json.dumps()?
options: They are identical, just aliases for the same function
json.dump() is for reading, json.dumps() is for writing
json.dump() writes JSON to an open file; json.dumps() returns a JSON string instead
json.dumps() only works with lists, never dictionaries
questions.explain: The 's' in dumps/loads stands for 'string' — those versions work with strings in memory, not files.

questions.q: After converting orders.csv rows to JSON with csv.DictReader + json.dump(), why are fields like quantity still quoted strings in the JSON output?
options: csv.DictReader never converted them to numbers, so there were no numbers to write in the first place
JSON format cannot represent numbers at all
json.dump() always converts every value to a string
Only customer_name can ever be a string in JSON
questions.explain: JSON can represent real numbers, but only if you convert the Python value yourself before dumping it.

questions.q: In this lesson's grouped-by-customer example, how many orders does customer_id 501 (Dana Whitfield) have in orders.csv?
questions.explain: Dana Whitfield appears on orders 1001, 1003, and 1018 — three separate orders.

options: Deletes a JSON file after reading it
Parses JSON from an open file back into a Python object
Writes a Python object as a JSON string
questions.explain: json.load() is the mirror of json.dump() — file in, Python object out.

questions.q: Why is defaultdict(list) useful when grouping orders by customer_id or region?
options: It automatically creates an empty list for a new key the first time it's used, so you don't have to check if the key already exists
It is required by json.dump() for any nested structure
It sorts the resulting dictionary alphabetically
questions.explain: Without defaultdict, you'd need an explicit check-and-create step before appending to each key's list.
